content:
It seems dual decorated lemmas like

@[to_dual ne_of_gt]
lemma ne_of_lt (h : a < b) : a ≠ b := fun he => absurd h (he ▸ lt_irrefl a)

get improperly displayed in VS Code

Note here we are talking about lt and not gt. Has anyone else reproduced this?

Where are you seeing this? Is the bug that it shows the hover for ne_of_gt when it should show that of ne_of_lt? Or did you miss that these are two different declarations (one of them generated by to_dual)? I cannot reproduce the first issue.
Better screenshot outside of namespace Nat
Is your point that it's b < a rather than a > b? That's intentional
See https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/naming.html#lattices for an explanation of this naming convention in mathlib.

Mathlib tries to always use < instead of >, because this avoids the need to rewrite between them. So, we gave gt a special meaning in identifier names, basically meaning lt, but with the arguments swapped.

Where are you seeing this?

I already mentioned VS Code and included a screenshot of the tooltip. Perhaps you mean which version? It is the most recent version of VS Code at least, not sure when the plugin should auto-update. But I can also reproduce it just fine online:

Or did you miss that these are two different declarations (one of them generated by to_dual)?

I am fully aware there are two different declarations and explaining that the one that is displayed as documentation to the other one is incorrect. You can see we display the docstring of lt for gt and I believe the reason is that the docstrings don't transfer in the dual auto-generation process.

Is your point that it's b < a rather than a > b? That's intentional

I am not sure it should be intentional to show b < a for a theorem with the gt name. After all the two naming conventions are separated and not freely mixed like this.

Mathlib tries to always use < instead of >, because this avoids the need to rewrite between them.

Yes, this makes complete sense and I think sooner or later everyone is aware of this.

So, we gave gt a special meaning in identifier names, basically meaning lt, but with the arguments swapped.

Hmmm, I am not sure how many people can get tripped by this. After all the point of using gt is to represent > and Mathlib can prefer and use lt theorems rather than gt ones. I understand the underlying point that ultimately we want everything to be lt but is there no way to pass a correct docstring to the lt version adding one or more of these technical decisions? Or maybe a single sentence "This theorem is generated as a dual and thus has its direction swapped."?

In short: I think the entire gt replacement with < in docstrings is some technical detail that a close-up developer might prefer but an outsider or someone just following truly standard conventions can easily get confused by. This often happens in software engineering where a developer can get too close up with the changed they do to the extend that their context shifts away from what would be more natural when taking a step back.
I think some time ago mathlib declared that its convention is that both "gt" and "lt" in the name represents <, and the difference is only in the argument order.
It is not an artifact of to_dual-generated theorems. Hand-written theorems in Mathlib follow this convention as well

Also let me frame the same question in the following way: if gt is something we want to get rid of and is internally just swapped arguments of < + we have the convention to describe gt as lt in documentation, then why not just drop the ne_of_gt entirely instead of transferring documentation for it that doesn't relate to it? Having both gt and lt and maintaining only documentation for lt seems more confusing choice than just having lt as both API and documentation.

Plamen Dimitrov said:

You can see we display the docstring of lt for gt and I believe the reason is that the docstrings don't transfer in the dual auto-generation process.

but is there no way to pass a correct docstring to the lt version adding one or more of these technical decisions?

The theorem ne_of_gt (and also its dual ne_of_lt) does not have a docstring. Do you mean the type or signature of the theorem?

Aaron Liu said:

Plamen Dimitrov said:

You can see we display the docstring of lt for gt and I believe the reason is that the docstrings don't transfer in the dual auto-generation process.

but is there no way to pass a correct docstring to the lt version adding one or more of these technical decisions?

The theorem ne_of_gt (and also its dual ne_of_lt) does not have a docstring. Do you mean the type or signature of the theorem?

Signature indeed, thanks for the refinement. I was just pointing out at the tooltip I see but this is not precise enough so nice catch.

So signature and naming convention.

Plamen Dimitrov said:

then why not just drop the ne_of_gt entirely instead of transferring documentation for it that doesn't relate to it? Having both gt and lt and maintaining only documentation for lt seems more confusing choice than jsut having lt as both API and documentation.

If by "documentation" here you mean the signature as well then I don't understand what you are suggesting here. If we remove ne_of_gt then we won't be able to use it when proving other theorems. The type signature is what actually matters when you use it, the name is just a name and it could have just as well been called foobar or flip_flops. The reason we chose ne_of_gt over any other name is to make it easy to guess the name given the statement you want (so when you need to prove a < b → b ≠ a you can figure out which theorem you want) and to make it easy to guess the statement given only the name (so when you see this theorem referenced in a proof you can figure out what is happening in the proof).

note that ne_of_lt and ne_of_gt are actually different theorems, ne_of_lt says a < b → a ≠ b, with the order of a and b the same between < and ≠, and ne_of_gt says b < a → a ≠ b, with the order of the a and b reversed between < and ≠

Part of the documentation is embedded into the function name which is carefully chosen to reflect its purpose so there is indeed some documentation already within the signature.

If we remove ne_of_gt then we won't be able to use it when proving other theorems.

Some of the main arguments here were that ne_of_gt is internally just ne_of_lt. You can use that instead.

The type signature is what actually matters when you use it, the name is just a name and it could have just as well been called foobar or flip_flops.

Theoretically yes but in software engineering practice including ease of use, technical debt, and maintainability I would say a strong no to this.

The reason we chose ne_of_gt over any other name is to make it easy to guess the name given the statement you want (so when you need to prove a < b → b ≠ a you can figure out which theorem you want) and to make it easy to guess the statement given only the name (so when you see this theorem referenced in a proof you can figure out what is happening in the proof).

If I would need to prove a < b → b ≠ a I would guess a name like ne_of_lt and if I want to prove a > b → b ≠ a I would have guessed ne_of_gt which ends up written via b < a in the signature. However, I think most people will associate gtwith > and get confused by this while paying less attention to the order of "a" and "b" if they build an internal model that associates gt with > which I might be wrong but recall seeing in some other theorems.

So I guess it makes complete sense to map two different but very similar and dual operators like < and > into one binary operation with more clearly expressed symmetry and less need of swapping the order. I just hope that then gt is consistently mapped into a < b throughout Mathlib so that it never brings about the associations between gt and >. In any case I will report back here if I encounter contradiction where gtnow suddenly means > and thus there will always be more cognitive load in separating which is which.

Aaron Liu said:

note that ne_of_lt and ne_of_gt are actually different theorems, ne_of_lt says a < b → a ≠ b, with the order of a and b the same between < and ≠, and ne_of_gt says b < a → a ≠ b, with the order of the a and b reversed between < and ≠

Plamen Dimitrov said:

Some of the main arguments here were that ne_of_gt is internally just ne_of_lt. You can use that instead.

@Plamen Dimitrov, did you actually read what @Aaron Liu wrote?

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

If we remove ne_of_gt then we won't be able to use it when proving other theorems.

Some of the main arguments here were that ne_of_gt is internally just ne_of_lt. You can use that instead.

@Plamen Dimitrov, did you actually read what @Aaron Liu wrote?

Sorry I guess I wasn't clear here. I mean that we can only make use of one of these two and only swap the order of the arguments if we ever need the other one. So by "ne_of_gt is internally just ne_of_lt" I don't mean that they are the same as the signature is clearly different, I mean that we can always use just one of them for all of our needs and having the other with this technical difference could confuse users.

Also my point about consistency remains, I think I have seen some cases of inconsistent use of this technical rule in the past and I hope at least such consistency is thoroughly respected.
you can't get from ne_of_lt to ne_of_gt just by switching argument order, you need additionally some kind of docs#Eq.symm

Aaron Liu said:

you can't get from ne_of_lt to ne_of_gt just by switching argument order, you need additionally some kind of docs#Eq.symm

Indeed, and we also don't have a b = a auxiliary theorem defined for each a = b inclusive theorem out there but instead define just one version and rely on extra Eq.symm step when needed which is quite cheap.
the reason we have one for ne_of_lt is that that's what you get when you take its order dual
a = b vs b = a is primarily decided on which of a or b is more complicated

Yaël Dillies said:

a = b vs b = a is primarily decided on which of a or b is more complicated

Yes, we can write just one version of a = b vs b = a based on some criterion like complexity (to the left) and only use Eq.symm when we need the other version. In the same way we can write just one version a < b vs b > a based on some criterion like canonicity of the lt/le direction and some swap+symm to get the other version when we need it. In other words we only keep one version in the code base and always obtain the other one via extra cheap beta reduction steps.

the reason we have one for ne_of_lt is that that's what you get when you take its order dual

One could also argue that there is a trivial duality in the transformations back and forth between a=b and b=a but of course the order duality here is less trivial and more studied.

Ok, in any case I was throwing ideas in here, I guess the current choices of including a well studied order duality make enough sense and people should simply be aware of the carefully selected arguments order even though this seems more like a Mathlib-implementation-related choice rather than the math it implements. Good enough of course.
